hmmt-nov-2011-team-01.title: Divisible by 3
hmmt-nov-2011-team-01.body:
Modulo $3$: $3^x\equiv0$, and $5,11,17\equiv-1$, $7,13,19\equiv1$. So the sum is $\equiv(-1)^x\cdot3+3\equiv3[(1)+(-1)^x]\equiv0\pmod3$. The sum exceeds $3$, so it is composite for every $x\ge1$. Answer $0$.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-nov-2011-team-02.title: Factor out $x-1$
hmmt-nov-2011-team-02.body:
$Q(x)=(x-1)\bigl(x^2+(p+1)x+1\bigr)$. We need the quadratic to have two distinct real roots, neither equal to $1$.

Distinct real: $(p+1)^2-4>0$, i.e. $p>1$ or $p<-3$. Root $1$: $1+(p+1)+1=0$ iff $p=-3$, which is not in the range. So the answer is all $p$ with $p<-3$ or $p>1$.

**Answer: $p\in(-\infty,-3)\cup(1,\infty)$**

hmmt-nov-2011-team-03.title: Shift to a polynomial with known roots
hmmt-nov-2011-team-03.body:
Let $Q(x)=P(x)-x-6$. Then $Q(5)=Q(11)=Q(17)=0$ and $Q$ is monic quartic with $x^3$-coefficient $-29$. By Vieta the roots sum to $29$, so the fourth root is $29-5-11-17=-4$. Hence $Q(x)=(x-5)(x-11)(x-17)(x+4)$.

The sum of the coefficients is $P(1)=Q(1)+1+6=(-4)(-10)(-16)(5)+7=-3200+7=-3193$.

**Answer: $-3193$**

hmmt-nov-2011-team-04.title: Factorizations
hmmt-nov-2011-team-04.body:
Distinct rational roots mean $P$ factors over the integers. Since $p_1,p_3$ are prime, the only factorizations are:
- $(p_1x-p_3)(x+1)$: $p_2=p_1-p_3$.
- $(p_1x+p_3)(x-1)$: $p_2=p_3-p_1$.
- $(p_1x-1)(x+p_3)$: $p_2=p_1p_3-1$.
- $(p_1x+1)(x-p_3)$: $p_2=1-p_1p_3<0$, impossible.

Case 1: $p_1=p_2+p_3$ forces $p_1$ odd and one of $p_2,p_3$ equal to $2$: twin prime pairs below $50$: $(3,5),(5,7),(11,13),(17,19),(29,31),(41,43)$, giving $6\cdot2=12$ polynomials. Case 2 is symmetric: $12$.

Case 3: $p_2=p_1p_3-1$. If $p_1,p_3$ are both odd, $p_2$ is even so $p_2=2$ and $p_1p_3=3$, impossible. So $p_1=2$ or $p_3=2$. For $p_1=2$: $p_2=2p_3-1$ prime with $p_3$ prime: $p_3=2,3,7,19$ giving $p_2=3,5,13,37$ (4 solutions). Likewise $4$ for $p_3=2$, and $(2,3,2)$ is counted twice: $7$.

Total $12+12+7=31$.

**Answer: 31**

hmmt-nov-2011-team-05.title: Each quadrant independently
hmmt-nov-2011-team-05.body:
The operations only rotate within each of the four $2\times2$ quadrants, and the quadrants are independent. Within one quadrant there are $2^4=16$ colorings, which fall into orbits under the rotation of the four cells: all red; all blue; one blue (3 red); one red (3 blue); two adjacent blue (and two red); two opposite blue. That is $6$ orbits.

So the number of distinct colorings of the whole grid is $6^4=1296$.

**Answer: 1296**

hmmt-nov-2011-team-06.title: Two transition points
hmmt-nov-2011-team-06.body:
No lower-case can be followed by upper-case, so the row is upper-case then lower-case; likewise it is green then yellow. We must pick the position where the colors switch from green to yellow and where the case switches from upper to lower.

Each switch is a position between consecutive letters, or at the ends; the conditions force: at least one green (the first C is green), at least one lower-case (the last C is lower-case), and some C both upper-case and yellow, so the last green C comes strictly before the last upper-case C. Writing $g$ for the number of green Cs and $u$ for the number of upper-case Cs: $1\le g<u\le9$, so the count is $\binom92=36$.

**Answer: 36**

hmmt-nov-2011-team-07.title: Add a sixth pair
hmmt-nov-2011-team-07.body:
Add a sixth pair $Cc$ whose colors are forced: the upper-case C gets the one unused color among the first five upper-case Cs, and the lower-case c the one unused color among the first five lower-case ones. Any coloring of the first five pairs extends uniquely, so we count colorings of six pairs in which the upper-case Cs use all six colors and the lower-case cs use all six colors, with the first five pairs having different colors in each pair.

There are $6!=720$ ways to color the upper-case Cs. For the lower-case:
- If the sixth pair has different colors, the lowers form a derangement of the uppers: $D_6=265$.
- If the sixth pair has the same color, the sixth lower is forced and the other five form a derangement relative to their uppers: $D_5=44$.

Total $720(265+44)=222480$.

**Answer: 222480**

hmmt-nov-2011-team-08.title: Use symmetry about the diameter $GB_3$
hmmt-nov-2011-team-08.body:
$GB_3$ is a diameter. $A_2,A_3$ are symmetric about it, as are $B_1,B_5$. So lines $B_1A_2$ and $B_5A_3$ are mirror images and meet on line $GB_3$; hence they meet at $G_2$, and $B_1,A_2,G_1,G_2$ are collinear.

Then $\angle GG_2G_1=\angle GG_2B_1$, an angle formed by two chords meeting inside the circle: it equals half the difference of the arcs $\overset{\frown}{GB_1}$ and $\overset{\frown}{B_3A_2}$. Arc $GB_1=60^\circ$ and arc $B_3A_2=180^\circ-144^\circ=36^\circ$. So the angle is $\frac{60^\circ-36^\circ}2=12^\circ$.

**Answer: $12^\circ$**

hmmt-nov-2011-team-09.title: Homothety at the midpoint of $AC$
hmmt-nov-2011-team-09.body:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$. Then $MG=\frac13MB$ and $MG'=\frac13MB'$, so $GG'=\frac13BB'$. And $BB'$ is twice the altitude from $B$ to $AC$.

By Heron, $s=18$ and $[ABC]=\sqrt{18\cdot9\cdot8\cdot1}=36$. The altitude is $\frac{2\cdot36}{17}=\frac{72}{17}$, so $BB'=\frac{144}{17}$ and $GG'=\frac{48}{17}$.

**Answer: $\frac{48}{17}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-team-10.title: Cyclic quadrilateral
hmmt-nov-2011-team-10.body:
By the law of cosines $\cos\angle G_2G_1G_3=\frac{49+225-169}{2\cdot7\cdot15}=\frac12$, so $\angle G_2G_1G_3=60^\circ$ and $G_1G_4$ bisects it. The bisector meets the circumcircle of $G_1G_2G_3$ again at the midpoint of arc $G_2G_3$, which lies on the perpendicular bisector of $G_2G_3$ as does $G_4$. Hence $G_4$ is that point and $G_1G_2G_4G_3$ is cyclic.

Then $\angle G_4G_3G_2=\angle G_4G_1G_2=30^\circ$, so $G_2G_4=G_4G_3=\frac{13}{\sqrt3}$. Let $G_5G_2=x$, $G_5G_4=y$. Triangles $G_5G_4G_2\sim G_5G_1G_3$ give $\frac{x}{y+13/\sqrt3}=\frac{13/\sqrt3}{15}=\frac{y}{x+7}$. From the first equality $y=\frac{15\sqrt3}{13}x-\frac{13}{\sqrt3}$; substituting into the second equality and dividing by $x$ gives a linear equation with $x=\frac{169}{23}$.

(A coordinate computation confirms $G_2G_5\approx7.348=\frac{169}{23}$.)

**Answer: $\frac{169}{23}$**
